text: Brady Rasso is a passionate Student at the university of Nebraska-Lincoln. He is studying sports media and communications as well as business administration. He works as a student equipment manager with Nebraska athletics. Rasso enjoys going to concerts, playing sports and attending other events.

title: A Tale of two halfs the Nebraska basketball seasson
text:
After the best season in the Fred Hoiberg era, Nebraska basketball entered the year with expectations of returning to the Big Dance. With a newly assembled roster through the transfer portal and key players returning, it seemed like there was no way this team wouldn’t at least make a push for an at-large bid. After a first half that set them up for success the rest of the season, we saw a completely different team down the stretch—one that not only destroyed the Huskers’ tournament dreams but also failed to qualify for the Big Ten tournament. So, what happened between the first and second half of the season?

The Huskers were one of the streakiest teams in the country, with the ability to get hot and torch opponents from three, going on long win streaks—or go ice cold and struggle to take care of lesser competition, leading to multiple consecutive losses. This inconsistency didn’t just apply to game results, but to other aspects of their play as well. Nebraska lived and died by the three a season ago—but how did that carry over?

And when the moments were the brightest, the shots from behind the arc just weren’t falling. So, with a team that Coach Hoiberg built around size—featuring bigger players at nearly every position—did that size actually translate into rebounding production for the Cornhuskers? More importantly, how did that impact their ability to close out defensive possessions with rebounds or create second-chance opportunities on offense?

We did see some improvement in rebounding during the second half of the season, but at best, Nebraska was average when it came to controlling the glass. And being just average in that area—especially with the size this roster had—isn’t going to cut it when it’s time to win big games. So what does Fred Hoiberg need to do in the portal to make a real run at the Big Dance next year? Find quality shooters—and bring in dominant bigs who can consistently clean the glass.

title: Florida the obvious National Champions
text:
From a first-round exit to one of the best seasons in school history, the Florida Gators dominated all year—despite being ranked near the bottom of the AP Poll to start the season. But should they have been ranked that low to begin with? Florida managed to retain all its key pieces, including Walter Clayton Jr. and Alex Condon, while also adding impactful transfers like Aijah Martin and Rueban Chinyelu. With a complete and reloaded roster, being ranked 21st in the country to start the season seems low. Regardless of what the AP Poll indicated, it was clear from the start that the Florida Gators were destined to compete for the national championship.
The Gators had a strong offensive balance, with four players averaging over 10 points per game, making it possible for anyone to take over on any given night. Leading the charge was First Team All-American Walter Clayton Jr., who averaged 18.3 points per game while shooting an impressive 45% from the field and 39% from three-point range. Clayton consistently carried the offensive load, but how did the team as a whole stack up against the rest of the NCAA?


Code
ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = ncaascatter, aes(x = fieldgoalpercentage, y = pointspergame),color="lightgrey") +
  geom_point(data = gatorboy, aes(x = fieldgoalpercentage, y = pointspergame),color="#FA4616")+
  
  geom_vline(xintercept = 44.34716) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 73.15875) +
  geom_text(
    aes(x = 35, y = 40, label = "Bad at Scoring, Not Efficient "),
    color = "black"
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(x = 50, y = 90, label = "Elite scoring , Super Efficient"),
    color = "black") +
  labs(
    title = "The Gator offense took over games",
    subtitle = "The Florida offense was elite among  the country this season",
    x = "Field Goal Percentage",
    y = "Points Per Game",
     caption = "By: Brady Rasso | Source: hoopR"
  ) +
  geom_text(
  aes(x = 49, y = 85),
  label = "Florida",
  size = 3) +
theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 8),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
     plot.title.position = "plot"
  ) 









Not only did Florida average more points than the NCAA league average, but they also shot the ball significantly better, placing them in elite company. When the Gators were firing on all cylinders, they were nearly impossible to stop. One thing clearly stands out when reviewing Florida’s season—it highlights just how dominant they truly were. So, what exactly was the Gators’ X-factor?


Code
iron(
  waffle(
    gatorwaffle,
    rows = 3,
colors = c("#FA4616", "white")
)+
  labs(
  title = "The Gators are the most dominant team in the second half ",
     subtitle = "Florida when leading at half become unbeatable"
 )+
   theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
     plot.title.position = "plot"
),
  waffle(
    gatorwaffle2,
    rows = 3,
     colors = c("#0021A5"))+
      labs(
           x= "1 square = 1 Win",
         caption = "By: Brady Rasso | Source: hoopR"
      )
)









A perfect 25-0 record when leading at halftime is a major reason why Florida should have been considered a legitimate favorite to win the national championship. Their ability to take control early and consistently close out games was a defining strength. This trend carried into March as well, where the Gators went 2-0 in the NCAA Tournament when leading at the half. So, we know that Florida can score at will and rarely give up leads—but is that enough to support the championship narrative for this team? They say defense wins championships, so the question is: did the Gators lock down their opponents, or were they constantly forced to outscore other teams?


Code
ggplot() +
  geom_dumbbell(
    data = newncaadumbell,
    aes(y = reorder(team_location,avrgsteals), x = avrgblocks, xend = avrgsteals),
    size = 2,
    colour = "#000",
    colour_x = "#FA4616",
    colour_xend = "#0021A5"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Gator's rivaled others was defensive threat",
    subtitle = "<span style = 'color:Blue;'>Steals</span> are on the right, . If <span style = 'color:orange;'>Blocks</span> are on the right,. Florida was competitive with other teams for an elite defensive status ",
    y = "Team",
    x= "Blocks and steals Averages",
    caption = "By: Brady Rasso | Source: hoopR"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_textbox_simple(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 8),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.title.position = "plot"
  )

ℹ Please use the `linewidth` aesthetic instead.









What we can take away from this is that not only can Florida score the ball, but they can also make an impact on the defensive side as well. The Gators were right up there with teams known for playing tough defense.
Taking everything into consideration, I think this team was severely underrated from the beginning and put together a fantastic regular season. Once tournament time came around, it was well deserved that they earned a one seed. They stuck to their identity as a team that not only takes good shots but also makes them. Opponents struggled against the Gators—especially when Florida got a lead, as their opponents stood little chance of coming back.
Florida should have been the obvious pick to win the national championship from the start and deserved more respect as a team.
Will Florida be able to repeat as national champions next year?
